utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Indah Susanti.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one very brief matter, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, you will recall that on the very first day of the sitting in September Ms. Korner brought up the matter of scheduling, the further scheduling in this case. In the meantime, I spoke to our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, and they indicated that they will be filing the motion for rebuttal witnesses. And the assurances I got from Ms. Korner was that it would be filed by end of this month, and I would kindly like to put that on the record and ask the Trial Chamber to issue an order in that respect that -- or suggest to the Office of the Prosecutor that, indeed, they file this by the end of the month, which will give us the time to -- adequate time for prepare for these rebuttal witnesses, if, of course, the Trial Chamber decides to adhere to that request. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's correct, and that's fine. That's reasonable. But I just want to put on the record, we would like to reserve the right, however, if there is some future witness to come after the end of the month that raises something that might, in our view, deem it necessary to ask for a rebuttal regarding that witness, that at that time we would make a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So do I correctly infer what you have just said that you confirm Mr. Zecevic's understanding that you will be filing by the end of this month? Save for what you have just indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those that we now are aware of and have a position about, we will file by the end of the month. I just wanted to reserve for the possibility that something may occur with witnesses yet to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- that's understandable. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is -- there is an oversight on the part of the Chamber yesterday in terms of the pseudonym sheet. We forgot to order that it be entered as an exhibit, which we now do. So it's an exhibit and should be given a number under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, pseudonym sheet shall be given Exhibit 2D154, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We also have an another little matter to deal with before the witness comes in regarding the Prosecution's motion to reopen its case in-chief. This motion was filed by the Prosecution on the 26th of July, and the Prosecution asks to reopen in order to tender a number of documents from the bar table. The documents concerned are death certificates and other documents on which the Prosecution wishes to rely in order to establish the death of a number of individuals. The documents are further specified in confidential Annex A to the motion. Now, before taking a decision on this motion, the Chamber directs the Prosecution to provide the dates on which it sent out the Requests for Assistance to the respective countries, which led it to being provided with the documents in question. And we further direct the Prosecution to include information on any still outstanding Requests for Assistance pertaining to the proof of death database in this case. And, finally, we ask the Prosecution to provide us with at least a template translation of the documents. And this is to be filed by the close of business on Friday, the 30th of September. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we go into closed session so the witness could be conducted back to the stand by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the situation in Banja Luka in late 1991 yesterday. We saw some documents. And now can you tell us what the situation in the town of Banja Luka was in 1992; first and foremost, the security situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as for the security situation, it was complex in 1992, and the economic situation was difficult. Life was hard. The complexity of the security situation in Banja Luka is reflected in a large number of armed members of the military, also other persons armed with long-barrelled weapons. Automobiles without licence plates were driven or they had stolen licence plates from other cars. There was car theft. And public security staff were unable to stand up to such groups that were armed with long-barrelled weapons, because there were many. There were about 200 staff of -- at the police stations. The police officers were not trained for carrying out suitable activities, appropriate activities, against these perpetrators. They were trained, like me, for routine tasks. The core was about 4.000 men-strong, as far as I know. Then there was a large number of reserve soldiers. The military police was in charge of military personnel, including reserve forces. They had the right to check their IDs and carry out controls and arrest them, if necessary, as well as initiate proceedings against them. I said at the outset that the situation -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have to interrupt you. We'll come to this later. The armed men that you mentioned, what kind of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People armed with long barrels used to wear different sorts of uniforms: Camouflage, multi-coloured, all sort of uniforms with all sorts of insignia on their caps, on their uniforms, on parts of their uniforms. As for the economic situation in town, it was complex, as I have already mentioned. It meant that the companies were not working. There wasn't enough of raw goods. Markets were unavailable. There was almost no transport of goods into the area because the roads were blocked. The corridor was closed at the time. Only shops were open in town. However, the shelves were almost empty. There was a little bit of food and other products necessary for daily life. The salaries were very low. There was inflation. I'll give you an example. My salary was sufficient for me to buy some of the things, some of the food, in shops today. However, the day after, I could not buy even a box of matches with the remainder of the money, or, for instance, some handkerchiefs. Also, public transport was not functioning properly in town. It was limited because of the lack of fuel. On the positive side, schools were open, elementary schools, high schools, and the university. The movement in town was allowed until the moment of curfew, which means that from 2200 until 5.00 in the morning nobody was allowed to move through town. As I said, the remuneration, or, as we say it, salaries, were low while the inflation was high. People used to take their own belongings from their houses, for instance, pots or plates, sometimes even furniture; those items of furniture that could be taken out of the house. All this clearly paints a picture of a very hard economic situation in the town of Banja Luka. Let me tell you another thing. My wife worked in another company. She's highly qualified, university education. However, that company would work for two days. Then it would stop working for three days. Her salary was very low, or there was no salary at all. And, believe me, this is a company situated 5 to 7 kilometres from the centre of the town, the part where we live. Every day she went there on her bike, regardless of the weather conditions, rain, snow, or ice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe the situation regarding the electrical energy supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation with the electricity was variable, if I may put it that way. Sometimes there was electricity. And when there were combat actions around Jajce and the hydropower plant, there was no electricity in the whole of Banja Luka. Sometimes it was on; sometimes it was off. So we, the citizens, the population, didn't know when exactly there would be electricity or not, so we tried to make our use most efficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't mention the part of the town where you live, but could you describe the composition of the position there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The part of the town where I live, even before the war, it was mixed, as we say. Multi-ethnic. I'm not going to say which part of town exactly it is. During the war in 1992, the ethnic composition of that part of town remained the same, I think. The same as it was before the war during the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the power supplies were cut, how was it done? Was it from part to part of town or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, I think that nobody could know which parts of town, which streets, which house, houses, housed Bosniaks or Croats or others. There were no rules related to the cut-offs. There were some days when, for example, a part of town would be without electricity, a particular settlement or even a particular street, but there were no cut-offs or restrictions, if you'd permit me to say, for the parts in town -- for the parts of the town where only Bosniaks or Croats lived without any Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were some restrictions in the bus traffic. However, the public transport in Banja Luka did function at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The public transport in Banja Luka functioned with some restrictions. Some of the lines would have daily frequency or five or ten buses a day. However, when the service was restricted. Sometimes it would be only one departure a day, or even the line would be down for several days. It all depended on the availability of the fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you describe the situation related to the market-place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The market-place in Banja Luka was one of the best supplied market-places in that part of the state. However, due to combat activities -- and, excuse me, let me tell you one more thing. The surroundings of Banja Luka is a well-known agriculture area. In 1992, the market-place in Banja Luka was not well supplied. You could find some things but not very many. I think that the reason for that is the fact that many people were mobilised. Fields were not tilled. There were some vegetable gardens around houses, but the market-place was in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the movement about town was allowed except during the curfew. Can you tell us whose decision was it? Which organ proclaimed the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already stated, the curfew was on between 10.00 in the evening and 5.00 in the morning. I know that it was proclaimed by a decision by the Secretariat for National Defence. There were some exceptions to the curfew. Members of the police were free to move about, as well as the military police and also, as far as I can remember, members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then could you specify who was subject to the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the name itself implies, curfew, or "police hour" in B/C/S, means that nobody is allowed to move around between 10.00 in the evening and 5.00 in the morning, and it goes for all the citizens of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this decision promulgated by the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of this decision by the Secretariat for National Defence whereby the curfew was introduced was to prevent movement during the night, movement of people armed with long barrels in all sorts of uniforms. I already stated that they had all sorts of uniforms, all sorts of insignia, on their caps, on parts of their uniforms, shooting around the town, activating of explosive devices in streets, in courtyards, shooting in the air, and so on and so forth. In short, in order to ensure the security of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was authorised to issue permits to move about the town during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The permits authorising movement during the curfew were issued by the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who was authorised to issue permits to move outside Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The movement outside of Banja Luka towards other places was also subject to the decisions and permits issued by the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether, in Banja Luka town, there were any police check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I used to work in the relevant service. The police check-points were established and positioned on major roads, or, more precisely, on all the entry and exit points from Banja Luka. There were check-points on exits from Banja Luka. First location 0, as we used to call it. That is the intersection towards Mrkonjic Grad, Skender Vakuf, and Jajce. The second check-point was established in the territory of the police station -- I apologise. There was a check-point in the territory of the central police station. Then there was another check-point in the territory of the police station Mejdan. It was positioned at the Mejdan viaduct, as we call it. I'm not going to go into details about the exact position. Then there was the settlement of Vrbanja, where Muslims, Bosniaks were a majority population. And then there was also the settlement of Debeljaci, where Croats were majority population. And then towards Celinac, Kotor Varos, and further on. The third check-point was established at the Prijedor intersection, or Prijedor loop, as we call it. It was close to the prison. The Tunjice prison. That is the exit point towards Prijedor, Gradiska, Laktasi, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your estimate, how far were those check-points from the centre of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the check-points were maybe some 5 kilometres from the centre of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that the three check-points belonged to the territorial jurisdiction of the police stations Centar, Budzani [phoen], and Mejdan. Could you tell us to which organisational units belonged the policemen manning the check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already stated that the check-points belonged to different police stations. Centar, Mejdan, and Budzak. The police stations Centar, Mejdan, and Budzak, belonged to the public security station Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic composition of those police stations, especially Budzak and Mejdan, after the 1st of April and for the remainder of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I address the ethnic composition of police stations, let me say that the Mejdan Police Station used to cover an area with a large number of Bosniaks, so the ethnic composition of this police station reflected the ethnic composition of the population. You have to bear in mind that the territory of the Mejdan Police Station included two settlements with majority Bosniak population, Vrbanja and Debeljaci. In Debeljaci there was a majority of Croats. Further on, the Budzak Police Station had a mixed composition because there were many Croats living there. The Centar Police Station was rather mixed. There were Serbs in the previous two stations as well. However, in the centre there were all sorts of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of your answer relating to the situation in Banja Luka, you said that the police force was insufficient to deal with the situation. So could you tell us whether measures and activities were undertaken against the perpetrators of criminal offences in this particular situation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that against the perpetrators of criminal offences, as well as the gravest of crimes, such as murders, throwing of explosives, shooting in the air, measures envisaged by law were undertaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, deprivation of liberty, criminal prosecution, drafting of criminal reports, and reports submitted to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you maybe remember some of the names or some of the criminal groups that were prosecuted at the time for the gravest criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, Banja Luka town consists of a number of settlements. I'm not going to say any names. So each part of town had its own criminals, if I can put it that way. It was a long time ago, to be honest. But I do remember some of the people that were prosecuted, people who were bent on creating chaos in the town. There was Mandic, Javorac, then Java Goran, Kajkuta, Palackovic. Vedran Palackovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move into closed session so that the witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask just a few questions. My name is Slobodan Zecevic, and I defend Mr. Mico Stanisic. We haven't been introduced yet and I wanted to introduce myself. Sir, today, on page -- I think it was page 20, you mentioned check-points established in the suburbs of Banja Luka at three different places. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the action executed by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had the code-name Check-Point 91?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You should always make a short pause between my question and your answer because I have to have enough time to switch off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about this action, Check-Point 91? Do you remember when it started and what was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, the introduction of check-points at certain locations in the Banja Luka town, and I mentioned three locations, was aimed at the prevention of the armed formations, members of the TO and other armed groups, as well as individuals, carrying long barrels, as well as civilians armed with long barrels. The idea was that they should not be able to enter or exit the town or certain settlements and disturb the public order by opening fire at facilities and buildings, by shooting in the air, by throwing explosive devices, and by other means. The task of the check-point was to prevent the transfer of stolen vehicles without number plates or with stolen number plates, et cetera. Also, in my opinion, it was important, and an example for this was the Mejdan Police Station where the majority of the inhabitants were Bosniaks, it was important to prevent the arrival of armed individuals wearing different uniforms, opening fire at various buildings, throwing explosive devices in certain houses, and so on and so forth. So the check-points had a very important role. So it was impossible for armed individuals to go around, to exercise their criminal behaviour, or even endanger human lives. Also, various goods were being smuggled through the town, and it was also one of the tasks of the check-points to prevent that; for instance, trafficking of foods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your exhaustive explanation. You said that some individuals were prevented from entering the town or some of the settlements and to display -- and from displaying their criminal behaviour and endangering human lives. I think that you said that it wasn't possible to prevent it 100 per cent but that it was prevented to a large degree. Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course, somebody will always be able to pass through. However, there was a positive reception among the population, among the citizens, and it gave them a certain dose of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when I asked you about Check-Point 91, which was the action carried out by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP, do you remember whether the check-points were established for the first time sometime in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The authority vested in the members of the Ministry of Interior manning the check-points and the official steps that they were undertaking at the check-points, was it all envisaged by the Law on the Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All actions undertaken by the policemen at check-points were in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs, or, in other words, they were actions undertaken in relation to non-uniformed individuals; that is, civilians. Ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. Was one of the actions undertaken checking of identity, establishing of someone's identity? Was another of the actions, for instance, checking the vehicles, the trunks of the vehicles, checking the documents? Are those the actions that you claim were in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. They are the actions stipulated by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One more question on this subject. Were you aware, did you have any information, or are you aware of any instructions in relation to this, that at the check-points citizens would be treated differently depending on their ethnicity? Do you know if anything like that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. But I'm certain that once the ID papers would have been checked, nobody would have been accorded a different treatment depending on their ethnicity. All the official actions undertaken at the check-points were strictly in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs, bylaws. And all the citizens were treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These were all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross examination by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that last question from Mr. Zecevic, Witness. You personally were never involved at working at any of those check-points that were set up as part of Operation Check-Point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you cannot know of your own personal knowledge whether or not some individuals may have been mistreated or treated differently because of their ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I need to go into private session for my next series of questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we - thanks - we go into closed session so the witness can take the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you can help me with the correct terminology. Within the Banja Luka CSB there are various units like the -- the police department or police affairs, crime prevention and crime detection. What were they called within the CSB? Are they administrations, or sectors, or departments? What's the correct term I should use when I'm talking about those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right word to use is department, or sector. So police sector, crime police sector, department. Those same terms are still used today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You named several of them when you were talking to Mr. Aleksic. But there were a couple that -- that you may have overlooked. I want to confirm whether or not these were departments or sectors in the Banja Luka CSB in 1992. I take it there was an analysis and information section, or sector, or department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a department. And then within the department, one level lower, is another department. Or you can have sector and then department, and then the people who work on the execution of orders. Today's terminology, you have police sector. We even have numerical codes for all of them. So police sector is 01; crime police sector is 02; communications department is 03; personnel and legal affairs department, 04; financial department, 05. Then there are following departments: Fire prevention department; and, of course, there is the office of the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple of questions, because I've seen those numerical designators for the different departments or sectors or, I think, as they were called at the headquarters level of the RS MUP, administrations. And typically, I think, 01 is the police administration, police affairs and tasks; 2 is crime prevention and crime detection; 3, at least on one of the charts I saw, was for the fire and explosives; and communications was 4. Is that not consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how things are today. However, at the time, in 1992, we did not have all the departments, and I think -- no, I don't think, I know there were not administrations at the Banja Luka CSB. It's not an administration. It's a department. Police department, crime prevention and detection department, section for foreigners, financial department, personnel and legal affairs department, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I agree. When I mentioned "administrations," that's the term I've seen used in talking about those various units at the headquarters level but not at the CSB level. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there also in Banja Luka CSB -- I guess you mentioned financial. Materiel and financial. Was that one department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a department in charge of materiel affairs in the Security Services Centre. It was a group of people. Whether they were a department, I wouldn't know, but they were also in charge of technical matters, such as maintenance of vehicles, procurement of spare parts for vehicles, maintaining of hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The chiefs or the heads of these departments that we've been talking about, were they part of the -- of Chief Zupljanin's collegium in the CSB Banja Luka in 1992? Were those the people who would be part of what I've heard called the collegium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know what? We call it, in inverted commas, non-productive departments. While the operative departments are the police department and crime prevention and detection department. All other organisational units, be it foreigners, materiel and finance, legal and personnel, technical services, they have their chiefs but they are not authorised persons. They do not have the authority. They do not have shortened working years. Did they attend the collegiums? No, they did not. But whenever a need would arise, they would come later on to discuss a problem at hand, whether it would be purchase of spare parts for vehicles or for communication equipment or procurement of telex machines. And then they would talk to the chief of the centre or a person authorised by him but strictly about those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, are you saying what you referred to as the "non-productive departments," those are the people in the police who are not authorised officials? Does that mean people who -- they don't carry a gun, they don't have the power to make arrests, et cetera; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And within the 01, the police administration, police affairs and tasks, was the duty operations team part of that department in the Banja Luka CSB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the organisational structure in Banja Luka CSB in 1992, was the duty operations team under the police department, or sector, 01?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I had to stop you there. We're in open session and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we -- we would redact the relevant lines. There's -- apparently there's no correspondence between the lines as I read and on the other screens. But should we continue -- should we revert into private session to deal with this, or is the -- to continue your question, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we need to just so that I can get an answer on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you some general questions, if you know the answer, about the number of certain personnel in CSB and SJB Banja Luka in 1992. First of all, can you tell me in April/May of 1992 how many employees were there in the CSB Banja Luka? First of all, total number, counting both uniformed and operatives and the non-productive departments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the CSB, there were about 150 employees, of whom uniformed police, i.e., those wearing uniforms, were 12 to 13. In the white-collar crime prevention and detection, there were approximately 40, 45 [Realtime transcript read in error "four to 45"] employees who were authorised officials and who worked as plain-clothes officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify: The transcript has recorded "approximately four to 45." Is that what you said, or ... Did you say "four to five" or "four to 45"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Might I interrupt you briefly. Mr. Aleksic, we have been alerted that there's a matter that you wish to raise. A, do you still wish to raise it; and, B, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Five minutes at the end. And we're almost there. I believe that the matter is very important and that the Trial Chamber should know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, Mr. Aleksic says five minutes, but my experience is that you probably better allow for ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. That will be fine. I will stop in about five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, what about the SJB of Banja Luka? Can you tell us approximately the total number in April/May 1992, uniform, operatives, and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the Banja Luka SJB, there were about 300 authorised officials working there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give me a breakdown, in terms of authorised officials, the number of uniformed police officers versus operatives, detectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were perhaps 150 to 200 uniformed police officers. It is very difficult for me to talk about figures after such a long time. However, the total number of authorised officials was about 300, 200, 250, 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how about the non-authorised. Do you have any idea of the number in the SJB Banja Luka in April/May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Banja Luka SJB, now that we're talking about it, had the so-called non-productive units that belonged to the CSB, which means that the Banja Luka SJB had approximately 20 to 30 men. Believe me, I -- it's -- it's a very tall order to remember exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Did the numbers for both the CSB and the SJB increase later in 1992? Were additional authorised officials hired, or reserve policemen brought on board? I'm assuming that's what happened, but you tell me. Did the numbers go up for both the CSB and the SJB later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, we know very well, based on my testimony so far, that the solemn declaration was signed, so some of the officials, some of the employees, did not sign that solemn declaration. I wouldn't be able to tell you how many employees in numerical terms abandoned the service and abandoned the CSB. However, whether new people were hired, I really don't know. I only know that in all the reports that I can remember and of which I can speak from memory, Chief Zupljanin always emphasised the fact that the CSB had very few police officers, that -- that there were a lot of vacancies which had not been filled up, according to the organisational scheme of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll stop for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Witness, we have reached a point where we're about to take the adjournment for today, so we would go into closed session so that you may be escorted from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just for the record, before I forget, for the record, that Mr. Cvijetic has joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I know that this is not a simple technical procedure, but we have to move into private session. What I need to say needs to be said in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning at 9.00, this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of September 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
